# simoom documentation (full text)

> Every page of the simoom documentation (https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/) concatenated as plain markdown, for LLMs and coding assistants. simoom is a small, fast HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 server engine you build into Rust programs, with its own TLS 1.3 and nothing but the Rust standard library underneath.

---

Source: https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/

# simoom documentation

> simoom is an HTTP server you build into a Rust program; these guides show how to write services, add TLS, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, and keep the build small.

simoom serves HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, does its own TLS 1.3, and runs one event loop per CPU
core on epoll, io_uring, IOCP or kqueue. It uses nothing outside the Rust standard library and
needs no async runtime. If you have used a Rust web framework before, the main difference is
this: a service is a plain function that runs on the loop thread, so it answers fast work at
once and hands slow work to a pool or to your own threads.

## Where to find what

Read the guides in this order the first time; after that, jump to the one you need.

| you want to | go to |
|---|---|
| install simoom, run a first server and learn what a service is | [Getting started](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/getting-started.html) |
| read requests and build responses | [Services and replies](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/services-and-replies.html) |
| send requests to handlers by method and path | [Routing](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/routing.html) |
| call a database or another service without blocking the server | [Slow work](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/slow-work.html) |
| stream request and response bodies, push server-sent events | [Streaming and SSE](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/streaming-and-sse.html) |
| accept WebSocket connections | [WebSocket](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/websocket.html) |
| serve HTTPS with your certificates, mutual TLS, certificate rotation | [TLS](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/tls.html) |
| turn on HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 and tune them | [HTTP/2 and HTTP/3](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/http2-and-http3.html) |
| set limits, see what is refused, log requests | [Limits and security](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/limits-and-security.html) |
| choose threads and the I/O back end, stop gracefully, read counters | [Runtime](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/runtime.html) |
| make HTTP and WebSocket requests from Rust | [The client](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/client.html) |
| pick cargo features and see what each adds to the binary | [Features and size](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/features-and-size.html) |
| drive the HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, QUIC or TLS crates from your own I/O loop | [Sans-io crates](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/sans-io-crates.html) |
| give a coding agent the rules it needs to write simoom code | [For coding agents](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/coding-agents.html) |
| find quick answers to common questions | [FAQ](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/faq.html) |

The security model, every limit with its default, and the test results are in
[SECURITY.md](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/SECURITY.html). Measured numbers and how they were taken are on the
[benchmarks page](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/benchmarks/). The API reference is on
[docs.rs/simoom](https://docs.rs/simoom).

## How the pages are organized

Every guide starts with a short answer under its title, then shows code you can copy. Every Rust
example was compiled against simoom 0.1.0 with `--features full`; examples that need another
feature say so. Each guide ends with common questions.

## Common questions

### Which version do these docs describe?

simoom 0.1.0, the first release. The API can still change before 1.0; breaking changes will be
listed in the release notes.

### Is there a version of these docs for coding assistants?

Yes. The site publishes `llms.txt` (a summary with links) and `llms-full.txt` (every page as plain
markdown), and every HTML page has its markdown source next to it. The
[coding agents guide](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/coding-agents.html) lists the rules an assistant most often gets wrong.

### Where do I report a mistake in the docs?

Open an issue or a pull request on [GitHub](https://github.com/Cameleering/simoom). Security
problems go through a private advisory, as described in [SECURITY.md](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/SECURITY.html).

# Getting started with simoom

> Add simoom with `cargo add simoom`, write one function that answers a request, and call `start()`; a working HTTP server takes about ten lines.

simoom is a library, not a program: you add it to your own Rust project and it serves HTTP from
inside your process. This page installs it, runs a first server, and explains the one idea you
need before writing more: what a service is and where it runs.

## Install

simoom needs Rust 1.89 or newer and runs on Linux, Windows and macOS.

```sh
cargo add simoom
```

or in `Cargo.toml`:

```toml
[dependencies]
simoom = "0.1"
```

The default features give you HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 without TLS (h2c), WebSocket and the io_uring back
end. For TLS and HTTP/3 turn on `full`:

```toml
simoom = { version = "0.1", features = ["full"] }
```

There is nothing else to install: no C compiler, no OpenSSL headers, no async runtime.
[Features and size](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/features-and-size.html) lists every feature.

## A first server

```rust
use simoom::{Outcome, Reply, Request, Server, StaticReply};
use std::sync::Arc;

fn main() {
    let hello = Arc::new(StaticReply::new(200, &[("content-type", "text/plain")], b"Hello, World!"));
    let server = Server::builder()
        .listen("127.0.0.1:8080")
        .service(move |_req: &mut Request<'_>, reply: Reply<'_>| -> Outcome { reply.fixed(&hello) })
        .start()
        .expect("start the server");
    println!("listening on {}", server.local_addr());
    server.join();
}
```

Run it with `cargo run --release` and try it:

```sh
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8080/
curl --http2-prior-knowledge http://127.0.0.1:8080/   # the same server speaks HTTP/2 (h2c)
```

`StaticReply` serializes the response once, so every request is answered with one copy. It is the
fastest way to send a fixed answer, but any response works, as the next example shows.

## Routes and parameters

Most programs answer more than one path. A [`Router`](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/routing.html) sends each request to a handler
by method and path:

```rust
use simoom::{Outcome, Reply, Request, Router, Server};

fn main() {
    let router = Router::new()
        .get("/", |_: &mut Request<'_>, r: Reply<'_>| r.body_static(b"Hello, World!"))
        .get("/hello/:name", |req: &mut Request<'_>, r: Reply<'_>| -> Outcome {
            let name = req.param_str("name").unwrap_or("stranger");
            r.header("content-type", "text/plain").body(format!("Hello, {name}!"))
        });

    let server = Server::builder().listen("127.0.0.1:8080").service(router).start().expect("start");
    println!("listening on {}", server.local_addr());
    server.join();
}
```

`curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/hello/Ada` prints `Hello, Ada!`. An unknown path gets `404`, and a
known path with the wrong method gets `405` with an `allow` header.

## What a service is

A **service** is anything that takes a `&mut Request` and a `Reply` and returns an `Outcome`. A
closure with that signature is a service, and so is a `Router`. The `Reply` is finished exactly
once: with a body, with a deferred answer for later, with a stream, or with a WebSocket upgrade.
[Services and replies](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/services-and-replies.html) covers each.

The one rule to remember: **a service runs on the loop thread.** simoom runs one event loop per
CPU core, and each loop serves thousands of connections. While your function runs, that loop
does nothing else. So a service must answer in microseconds and must not block: no database
calls, no file reads, no `sleep`, no locks held for long.

There is no `async` and no `.await`. Slow work goes somewhere else:

- to simoom's bounded offload pool with `simoom::blocking` or `Reply::offload`;
- or to your own threads with `Reply::defer`, answering later from any thread.

[Slow work](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/slow-work.html) shows all three. If a handler blocks anyway, a watchdog notices and
moves that route to the offload pool, but that is a safety net, not a plan.

## Stopping the server

`start()` returns a `ServerHandle` once every loop is running. `join()` waits for the loops to
exit; `stop(grace)` starts a graceful stop. Port `0` lets the OS pick a free port, which is handy
in tests:

```rust
use simoom::{Reply, Request, Server};
use std::time::Duration;

fn run() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let server = Server::builder()
        .listen("127.0.0.1:0") // port 0: the OS picks a free port
        .service(|_: &mut Request<'_>, r: Reply<'_>| r.body_static(b"ok"))
        .start()?;
    let addr = server.local_addr();
    // ... use the server ...
    server.stop(Duration::from_secs(5));
    server.join();
    Ok(())
}
```

Dropping the handle stops the server at once. [Runtime](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/runtime.html) explains what a graceful
stop does on each protocol.

## Where to go next

- [Services and replies](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/services-and-replies.html): reading requests, every way to answer.
- [Routing](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/routing.html): parameters, wildcards, 404 and 405.
- [Slow work](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/slow-work.html): databases and other services without blocking the server.
- [TLS](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/tls.html) and [HTTP/2 and HTTP/3](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/http2-and-http3.html): HTTPS and the newer protocols.
- [Features and size](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/features-and-size.html): the smallest build for a device or a function.
- [FAQ](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/faq.html).

## Common questions

### Do I need tokio or another async runtime?

No. simoom has its own event loops and no async runtime. Services are plain functions. You can
still use simoom inside a program that runs tokio for other work; they don't interact.

### Why does my handler signature need the explicit types?

Rust can't infer closure argument types for a generic trait bound, so a closure passed to
`service` or `Router::get` needs `&mut Request<'_>` and `Reply<'_>` written out. A named `fn`
with that signature works too.

### Which address should I listen on?

`127.0.0.1:8080` accepts connections from the same machine only. `0.0.0.0:8080` accepts them on
every IPv4 interface, and `[::]:8080` on IPv6. You can call `listen` more than once.

### How do I run the bundled examples?

From a checkout of the repository: `cargo run --release -p simoom --example hello -- 127.0.0.1:8080`.

---

Source: https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/services-and-replies.html

# How do I read requests and send responses in simoom?

> A service gets a borrowed `Request` and a `Reply`; read the request, then finish the reply once with a body, a stream, a deferred answer or an upgrade.

Everything in simoom is built on one trait, `Service`. This page shows the three ways to write a
service, what you can read from a `Request`, and every way to finish a `Reply`.

## Three ways to write a service

**A closure.** Any `Fn(&mut Request<'_>, Reply<'_>) -> Outcome + Send + Sync + 'static` is a
service. This is what most examples use.

**A function.** The same signature as a named `fn`:

```rust
use simoom::{Outcome, Reply, Request, Server};

fn hello(req: &mut Request<'_>, reply: Reply<'_>) -> Outcome {
    if req.method() != b"GET" {
        return reply.status(405).header("allow", "GET").empty();
    }
    reply.header("content-type", "text/plain").body_static(b"hello")
}

fn main() {
    let server = Server::builder().listen("127.0.0.1:8080").service(hello).start().unwrap();
    server.join();
}
```

**A struct.** Implement `Service` when the handler carries state. The service is shared by every
loop thread, so its state must be `Send + Sync`: atomics, `Mutex`, `RwLock` or read-only data.

```rust
use simoom::{Outcome, Reply, Request, Service};
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU64, Ordering};

struct Counter {
    hits: AtomicU64,
}

impl Service for Counter {
    fn call(&self, _req: &mut Request<'_>, reply: Reply<'_>) -> Outcome {
        let n = self.hits.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed) + 1;
        reply.body(format!("request number {n}"))
    }
}

fn build() -> simoom::Builder {
    simoom::Server::builder().listen("127.0.0.1:8080").service(Counter { hits: AtomicU64::new(0) })
}
```

Closures can capture shared state too. Clone an `Arc` for each closure that needs it:

```rust
use simoom::{Outcome, Reply, Request, Router};
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::sync::{Arc, RwLock};

fn router() -> Router {
    let store: Arc<RwLock<HashMap<String, String>>> = Arc::default();
    let reader = store.clone();
    Router::new()
        .put("/kv/:key", move |req: &mut Request<'_>, r: Reply<'_>| -> Outcome {
            let key = req.param_str("key").unwrap_or("").to_string();
            let value = String::from_utf8_lossy(req.body()).into_owned();
            store.write().unwrap().insert(key, value);
            r.status(204).empty()
        })
        .get("/kv/:key", move |req: &mut Request<'_>, r: Reply<'_>| -> Outcome {
            match reader.read().unwrap().get(req.param_str("key").unwrap_or("")) {
                Some(v) => r.body(v.clone()),
                None => r.status(404).body_static(b"not found"),
            }
        })
}
```

A lock held for a few microseconds is fine on the loop thread. A lock that waits on slow work is
not; see [Slow work](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/slow-work.html).

## Reading the request

A `Request` borrows from the connection's receive buffer, so reading it costs nothing. Most
accessors return bytes (`&[u8]`), because HTTP allows bytes that aren't UTF-8; the `_str`
variants return text.

```rust
use simoom::{Outcome, Reply, Request};

fn inspect(req: &mut Request<'_>, reply: Reply<'_>) -> Outcome {
    let method = String::from_utf8_lossy(req.method()).into_owned();
    let path = req.path_str();
    let page = req.query_param("page").and_then(|v| std::str::from_utf8(v).ok()).unwrap_or("1");
    let agent = req.header("user-agent").map(String::from_utf8_lossy).unwrap_or_default();
    let peer = req.peer_addr().map(|a| a.to_string()).unwrap_or_default();
    let body_len = req.body().len();
    reply.body(format!("{method} {path} page={page} agent={agent} peer={peer} body={body_len} bytes ({:?})", req.version()))
}
```

| method | returns |
|---|---|
| `method()`, `target()`, `path()`, `path_str()` | the method, the full target, the path before `?` (not percent-decoded) |
| `query()`, `query_param(name)` | the raw query string, one raw parameter |
| `header(name)`, `headers()` | the first header with that name (case-insensitive), all headers in order |
| `host()` | `Host` on HTTP/1.1, `:authority` on HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 |
| `version()` | `Version::Http10`, `Http11`, `H2` or `H3` |
| `body()`, `is_streamed()`, `take_body()` | the buffered body, or the streaming body source ([Streaming](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/streaming-and-sse.html)) |
| `trailers()`, `trailer(name)` | trailer fields of a buffered body |
| `param(name)`, `param_str(name)` | a value captured by the [router](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/routing.html) |
| `peer_addr()`, `local_addr()`, `listener()` | the client's address, the address it connected to, which listener accepted it |
| `is_secure()`, `tls()` | TLS or not, and the TLS session details ([TLS](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/tls.html)) |
| `is_websocket_upgrade()` | a valid WebSocket handshake ([WebSocket](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/websocket.html)) |
| `to_owned_request()` | an `OwnedRequest` copy that can move to another thread |

Bodies up to `Limits::body_buffer` (64 KiB by default) arrive whole before your service is
called, so `req.body()` has them. Larger bodies stream; `req.body()` is then empty and
`req.is_streamed()` is true. Percent-decoding is up to you: `simoom::percent_decode` does it.

## Finishing the reply

Set the status (default 200) and headers, then finish the reply with exactly one of these:

```rust
use simoom::{Outcome, Reply, Request, Response, StaticReply};
use std::sync::Arc;

fn finishers() {
    let _a = |_: &mut Request<'_>, r: Reply<'_>| -> Outcome { r.body(String::from("owned text")) };
    let _b = |_: &mut Request<'_>, r: Reply<'_>| -> Outcome { r.body(vec![1u8, 2, 3]) };
    let _c = |_: &mut Request<'_>, r: Reply<'_>| -> Outcome { r.body_static(b"no copy") };
    let _d = |req: &mut Request<'_>, r: Reply<'_>| -> Outcome { r.body_copy(req.body()) };
    let _e = |_: &mut Request<'_>, r: Reply<'_>| -> Outcome { r.status(204).empty() };
    let _f = |_: &mut Request<'_>, r: Reply<'_>| -> Outcome {
        r.send(Response::new(201).header("content-type", "application/json").body(r#"{"ok":true}"#))
    };
    let not_found = Arc::new(StaticReply::new(404, &[("content-type", "text/plain")], b"not found"));
    let _g = move |_: &mut Request<'_>, r: Reply<'_>| -> Outcome { r.fixed(&not_found) };
}
```

| finisher | use it for |
|---|---|
| `body(x)` | a `String`, `Vec<u8>` or static bytes, moved without a copy |
| `body_static(b"...")` | constant bytes; large ones go out without a copy on plain HTTP/1.1 |
| `body_copy(&[u8])` | bytes you only borrow |
| `empty()` | no body (`content-length: 0`) |
| `send(Response)` | an owned `Response` built elsewhere; its status and headers replace the reply's |
| `fixed(&StaticReply)` | a response serialized once at start-up, the fastest path |
| `defer()` | a `Responder` to answer later from any thread ([Slow work](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/slow-work.html)) |
| `blocking(req, f)`, `offload(req, f)` | run the work on the offload pool ([Slow work](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/slow-work.html)) |
| `stream()`, `sse()` | a `BodySink` for a streamed body ([Streaming](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/streaming-and-sse.html)) |
| `websocket(handler)` | accept a WebSocket upgrade ([WebSocket](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/websocket.html)) |

The type system keeps you honest: each finisher takes the reply by value, so you can't answer
twice. If a reply is dropped without being finished, the client gets a `500`.

Some details the server handles for you:

- **Framing headers** (`content-length`, `transfer-encoding`) are written by the server; setting
  them is ignored. `connection: close` closes the connection after the response.
- **Header names** go out in lower case. An invalid name or value (CR, LF, NUL) turns the
  response into a `500` instead of reaching the wire.
- **`HEAD`** requests get the headers of the `GET` response without the body.
- **Trailers** after the body: `.trailer("grpc-status", "0")` on the reply, or
  `Response::trailer`. HTTP/1.1 then uses chunked framing.

## The Outcome value

`Outcome` is informational: `Outcome::Done` when the reply was sent (or a stream or upgrade
started), `Outcome::Deferred` when the answer comes later. Finishers return the right one, so you
normally just return what they return. After `reply.defer()` you return `Outcome::Deferred`
yourself.

## Panics

A panic in a service is caught. The client gets a `500`, its connection closes, the panic is
counted in `ServerHandle::stats().panics`, and the loop goes on serving everyone else.

## Optional helpers

Small helpers live behind their own cargo features, so you only compile what you use:

| feature | module | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `cors` | `simoom::cors` | answers preflights and adds CORS headers around a service |
| `auth` | `simoom::auth` | Basic, Digest and Bearer authentication around a service |
| `cookies` | `simoom::cookie` | reads `Cookie`, writes `Set-Cookie` |
| `multipart` | `simoom::multipart` | parses `multipart/form-data` bodies |
| `conditional` | `simoom::conditional` | ETag, `If-None-Match`, `Last-Modified` and range requests |
| `compression` | `simoom::Compression` | gzip and deflate responses (`brotli`, `zstd` add those) |

A helper wraps your service. With the `cors` feature:

```rust
use simoom::cors::Cors;
use simoom::{Reply, Request, Server};

fn build() -> simoom::Builder {
    let api = |_: &mut Request<'_>, r: Reply<'_>| r.body_static(b"{}");
    Server::builder().listen("127.0.0.1:8080").service(Cors::new().allow_any_origin().wrap(api))
}
```

The [API reference](https://docs.rs/simoom) documents each helper.

## Common questions

### How do I return JSON?

Set the content type and send the text: `r.header("content-type", "application/json").body(json)`.
simoom has no JSON library, since it has no dependencies; use the serializer you already have
(for example serde_json in your own crate) and pass the resulting `String`.

### How do I read a path parameter or a query parameter?

`req.param_str("id")` for a `:id` route segment, `req.query_param("page")` for `?page=2`. Both
return the raw value; decode it with `simoom::percent_decode` when it can contain `%XX` escapes.

### Can a handler be async?

No. A service is a plain function that returns before the loop moves on. For work that waits,
use `Reply::defer` and answer from any thread, or the offload pool; see [Slow work](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/slow-work.html).

### Why does my response come back as a 500?

Three causes: the reply was dropped without a finisher, a header name or value was invalid, or
the status was outside 200 to 999. A panic in the handler gives a 500 too.

---

Source: https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/routing.html

# How do I route requests by path and method in simoom?

> Build a `Router` with `.get`, `.post` and friends; `:name` or `{name}` captures a segment, `*name` the rest, and wrong methods get 405 automatically.

`Router` is a service that picks a handler by method and path. It runs on the loop thread, so a
`404` or `405` costs a hash lookup or a short walk through a tree, never a trip to a pool.

## A router with every kind of route

```rust
use simoom::{Outcome, Reply, Request, Router};

fn router() -> Router {
    Router::new()
        .get("/health", |_: &mut Request<'_>, r: Reply<'_>| r.body_static(b"ok"))
        .get("/users/:id", |req: &mut Request<'_>, r: Reply<'_>| -> Outcome {
            let id = req.param_str("id").unwrap_or("");
            r.body(format!("user {id}"))
        })
        .get("/teams/{team}/members/{member}", |req: &mut Request<'_>, r: Reply<'_>| -> Outcome {
            let (team, member) = (req.param_str("team").unwrap_or(""), req.param_str("member").unwrap_or(""));
            r.body(format!("{member} of {team}"))
        })
        .get("/files/*path", |req: &mut Request<'_>, r: Reply<'_>| -> Outcome {
            let path = req.param_str("path").unwrap_or("");
            r.body(format!("you asked for {path}"))
        })
        .post("/users", |req: &mut Request<'_>, r: Reply<'_>| -> Outcome {
            r.status(201).body(format!("created from {} bytes", req.body().len()))
        })
        .route("OPTIONS", "/users", |_: &mut Request<'_>, r: Reply<'_>| -> Outcome {
            r.status(204).header("allow", "GET, POST, OPTIONS").empty()
        })
        .any("/echo", |req: &mut Request<'_>, r: Reply<'_>| -> Outcome {
            r.body(String::from_utf8_lossy(req.method()).into_owned())
        })
        .fallback(|req: &mut Request<'_>, r: Reply<'_>| -> Outcome {
            r.status(404).body(format!("nothing at {}", req.path_str()))
        })
}
```

Pass it to `Server::builder().service(router)`.

## Methods

`get`, `post`, `put`, `delete` and `patch` add a route for that method. `route(method, path,
handler)` takes any method name, and `any(path, handler)` (or `route("*", ...)`) matches every
method.

- A path that exists with another method gets **`405 Method Not Allowed`** with an `allow`
  header listing the methods that do exist.
- **`HEAD`** uses the `GET` route when there is no `HEAD` route; the client gets the headers
  without the body.
- A path that matches nothing gets **`404`**, or goes to the `fallback` handler if you set one.

## Path patterns

| pattern | matches | captured |
|---|---|---|
| `/health` | exactly `/health` | nothing |
| `/users/:id` or `/users/{id}` | `/users/42`, not `/users/42/posts` | `id` = `42` |
| `/files/*path` (last segment only) | `/files/a/b.txt`, also `/files/` | `path` = `a/b.txt` |

When several routes could match, literal segments win over parameters, and parameters win over
wildcards. So `/users/me` beats `/users/:id` for the path `/users/me`.

Paths without patterns go into a hash map; the others go into a tree of path segments.

## Captured values are raw

Paths are matched as the client sent them, without percent-decoding, and `param` returns the raw
bytes. Decode them when a value can contain escapes such as `%20`:

```rust
use simoom::{percent_decode, Outcome, Reply, Request, Router};

fn router() -> Router {
    Router::new().get("/search/:term", |req: &mut Request<'_>, r: Reply<'_>| -> Outcome {
        let raw = req.param("term").unwrap_or(b"");
        match percent_decode(raw) {
            Some(term) => r.body(term),
            None => r.status(400).body_static(b"bad escape"),
        }
    })
}
```

## Routes and slow handlers

Any service can be a route handler, including `simoom::blocking(...)` for work that must run on
the offload pool ([Slow work](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/slow-work.html)). The stall watchdog also works per route: if one
handler keeps blocking its loop thread, that route alone moves to the offload pool and comes back
once it is fast again. `Router::stalls_before_offload(n)` changes how many stalls that takes for
this router (`0` never moves a route).

## Common questions

### Can I nest routers or mount one under a prefix?

Not in 0.1.0. A `Router` matches the whole path, so put every route in one router, or write a
small service that looks at the first path segment and calls one of several routers. Since a
`Router` is a `Service`, `router.call(req, reply)` works from inside your own service.

### How do I add middleware such as logging or authentication?

Wrap the router in your own service that does the work and then calls `router.call(req, reply)`.
For access logs, `Builder::on_complete` is simpler and sees every request, including ones the
parser refuses ([Limits and security](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/limits-and-security.html)). The `cors` and `auth` features
offer ready-made wrappers ([Services and replies](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/services-and-replies.html#optional-helpers)).

### Does the router handle trailing slashes?

No: `/users` and `/users/` are different paths. Add both routes if you want both to work.

### Is there a limit on the number of routes?

No fixed one. Exact paths cost one hash lookup however many there are; patterns cost one step per
path segment.

---

Source: https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/slow-work.html

# How do I call a database or a service from a simoom handler?

> Never block the loop thread: wrap slow handlers in `simoom::blocking`, or use `Reply::offload`, or `Reply::defer` and answer later from your own threads.

simoom serves thousands of connections on each loop thread. A handler that waits for a database,
a file or another HTTP service stops every one of those connections while it waits. This page
shows the three ways to move that work off the loop, and the safety net for when a handler
blocks anyway.

## Which way to choose

| your situation | use |
|---|---|
| a handler that blocks (database, file, HTTP call) and you have no thread pool of your own | `simoom::blocking(f)` as the route handler |
| a handler that is usually fast but sometimes slow | `reply.blocking(req, f)` or `reply.offload(req, f)` on the slow branch |
| your program already has worker threads, queues or a runtime | `reply.defer()` and answer through the `Responder` from any thread |
| microseconds of CPU, no I/O | answer inline, as usual |

`blocking` and `offload` run on simoom's **offload pool**. `defer` doesn't touch the pool at all.

## The offload pool with `blocking`

`blocking` turns a function that takes an `OwnedRequest` and returns a `Response` into a service.
The request is copied, the function runs on a worker thread, and its response goes back to the
connection:

```rust
use simoom::{blocking, OwnedRequest, Response, Router};
use std::time::Duration;

fn router() -> Router {
    Router::new().get("/report/:id", blocking(|req: OwnedRequest| {
        let id = String::from_utf8_lossy(req.param("id").unwrap_or(b"")).into_owned();
        std::thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(200)); // stands for a database query
        Response::text(format!("report {id}"))
    }))
}
```

The pool is bounded, so overload can't pile up:

- Worker threads start on demand and exit after 10 seconds idle. The cap is
  `Limits::offload_threads`; the default `0` means 32 per CPU, between 512 and 1024.
- At most `Limits::offload_queue` jobs wait (default 4096).
- The pool measures how long jobs wait (CoDel). When waits keep growing past what the workers can
  absorb, new requests get a fast **`503` with `Retry-After`** instead of joining an endless
  queue. The target adapts to how long your jobs take, so 100 ms database calls are not refused
  just for being 100 ms long.
- A panic in the function becomes a `500`.

## Only the slow branch: `Reply::blocking` and `Reply::offload`

When a handler is fast most of the time, keep the fast path inline and offload only the slow one:

```rust
use simoom::{Outcome, Reply, Request, Response};

fn handler(req: &mut Request<'_>, reply: Reply<'_>) -> Outcome {
    if req.query_param("cached").is_some() {
        return reply.body_static(b"from cache"); // fast: answer inline
    }
    reply.blocking(req, |req| {
        // slow: runs on an offload worker
        Response::text(format!("computed for {}", req.path_str()))
    })
}
```

`Reply::offload` does the same but gives the worker the usual `Request` and `Reply`, so code
written as an inline service runs unchanged on the pool:

```rust
use simoom::{Outcome, Reply, Request};

fn handler(req: &mut Request<'_>, reply: Reply<'_>) -> Outcome {
    reply.offload(req, |req, reply| {
        // the same Request and Reply API, on a worker thread
        let size = req.body().len();
        std::thread::sleep(std::time::Duration::from_millis(50));
        reply.status(202).header("content-type", "text/plain").body(format!("accepted {size} bytes"))
    })
}
```

## Your own threads: `Reply::defer`

If your program already has workers (a job queue, a thread pool, an integration engine), copy the
request with `to_owned_request()`, take a `Responder` with `reply.defer()`, and send both to your
workers. The `Responder` can be sent to any thread and answers once:

```rust
use simoom::{Outcome, Reply, Request, Response, Server};
use std::sync::mpsc;

struct Job {
    request: simoom::OwnedRequest,
    responder: simoom::Responder,
}

fn run() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let (tx, rx) = mpsc::channel::<Job>();
    let tx = std::sync::Mutex::new(tx);

    // your own worker thread (or pool)
    std::thread::spawn(move || {
        for job in rx {
            if job.responder.is_cancelled() {
                continue; // the client left or the deadline passed
            }
            let answer = format!("done: {}", job.request.path_str());
            job.responder.send(Response::text(answer));
        }
    });

    let server = Server::builder()
        .listen("127.0.0.1:8080")
        .service(move |req: &mut Request<'_>, reply: Reply<'_>| -> Outcome {
            let job = Job { request: req.to_owned_request(), responder: reply.defer() };
            if let Err(mpsc::SendError(job)) = tx.lock().unwrap().send(job) {
                job.responder.send(Response::new(503).body("worker gone"));
            }
            Outcome::Deferred
        })
        .start()?;
    server.join();
    Ok(())
}
```

This is how [Cameleer](https://github.com/Cameleering/cameleer) embeds simoom: its own route
threads answer, and simoom's pool isn't involved. A few things to know:

- **`Responder::send` returns `false`** when the connection is already gone; the response is
  dropped.
- **Dropping a `Responder`** without sending gives the client a `500`.
- **`Responder::stream(head)`** starts a streamed response instead of a whole one.
- **Order on HTTP/1.1:** while a response is deferred, that HTTP/1.1 connection reads no further
  requests, so responses stay in order. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 streams carry on independently.

## Deadlines and cancellation

By default a deferred or offloaded reply may take as long as it likes. Set
`Limits::defer_timeout` to your service-level objective: when it expires before an answer has
started, the client gets **`504 Gateway Timeout`** and the late answer is dropped.

The worker can find out that its work is no longer wanted, because the client went away or the
deadline passed. `Responder::is_cancelled()` is one atomic load, cheap to poll between steps.
`Responder::on_cancel(f)` runs `f` once on cancellation, on the loop thread, so `f` must be quick:
set a flag or wake a thread.

```rust
use simoom::Responder;
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicBool, Ordering};
use std::sync::Arc;

fn watch(responder: &Responder) -> Arc<AtomicBool> {
    let stop = Arc::new(AtomicBool::new(false));
    let flag = stop.clone();
    responder.on_cancel(move || flag.store(true, Ordering::Relaxed));
    stop
}
```

## Tuning the pool

```rust
use simoom::{Limits, Server};
use std::time::Duration;

fn build() -> simoom::Builder {
    Server::builder().listen("0.0.0.0:8080").limits(Limits {
        offload_threads: 64,                           // what your database allows
        offload_queue: 1024,                           // jobs waiting before 503
        defer_timeout: Some(Duration::from_secs(10)),  // 504 after this
        inline_budget: Some(Duration::from_millis(2)), // watchdog budget per inline call
        ..Limits::default()
    })
}
```

Set `offload_threads` to the concurrency your backends can take: if your database allows 64
connections, more than 64 workers only queue inside the database driver instead of in simoom,
where overload turns into a clean `503`.

## The watchdog, a safety net

A handler that turns out slow (it blocks, or uses more than `Limits::inline_budget` of CPU, 1 ms
by default) is a **stall**. After `Limits::stalls_before_offload` stalls (5) within
`Limits::stall_window` (1 s), that route alone moves to the offload pool. Other routes stay
inline. After `Limits::stall_recovery` fast calls (64) there, it comes back.

The watchdog measures CPU time, not wall time, so a loop thread preempted on a busy machine isn't
mistaken for a slow handler. Each stall is logged once per route and counted in
`stats().stalls`.

The calls before the move still held their loop thread, so treat the watchdog as a seatbelt,
not as a way to avoid choosing. It needs the `watchdog` feature (on by default); a minimal edge
build can leave it out.

## Common questions

### Can I use async/await or tokio inside a handler?

Not directly: a service returns before the loop moves on. You can run tokio in your program and
hand it the work: take a `Responder` with `reply.defer()`, move it into a spawned task, and call
`responder.send(...)` when the future completes. `Responder` is a plain `Send` value.

### What happens when the offload pool is full?

New requests that need it get `503 Service Unavailable` with `Retry-After: 1` right away, and
`stats().overloaded` counts them. Requests already admitted keep their latency.

### Is `blocking` the same as `tokio::task::spawn_blocking`?

Similar idea, different shape: `blocking` wraps a whole handler, the pool is bounded with
admission control, and overload answers `503` instead of queueing without limit.

### How do I read a large request body in a slow handler?

On the pool, `OwnedRequest::read_body()` reads the whole body, and `take_body()` gives a
`std::io::Read` stream. See [Streaming and SSE](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/streaming-and-sse.html).

---

Source: https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/streaming-and-sse.html

# How do I stream bodies and server-sent events with simoom?

> `Reply::stream` and `Reply::sse` return a `BodySink` you write from any thread; large uploads arrive through a `BodySource` read off the loop thread.

Some responses are too large to build in memory, or never end: a log export, a progress feed, a
live dashboard. Some uploads are too large to buffer. simoom streams both directions with
backpressure, so a slow client slows the writer instead of filling memory.

## Streaming a response

`reply.stream()` sends the status and headers at once and returns a `BodySink` for the body. The
body goes out chunked on HTTP/1.1 and as DATA frames on HTTP/2 and HTTP/3. `BodySink` is `Send`
and implements `std::io::Write`, so a thread can write to it:

```rust
use simoom::{Outcome, Reply, Request};
use std::io::Write;

fn numbers(_: &mut Request<'_>, reply: Reply<'_>) -> Outcome {
    let mut sink = reply.header("content-type", "text/plain").stream();
    std::thread::spawn(move || {
        for i in 0..1000 {
            // write waits while 64 KiB are pending, so a slow client slows this thread
            if writeln!(sink, "line {i}").is_err() {
                return; // the client went away
            }
        }
        sink.finish();
    });
    Outcome::Done
}
```

At most `Limits::stream_buffer` bytes (64 KiB by default) are handed to the connection and not
yet sent. Past that, `write` waits. That is fine on your own thread or an offload worker and
**wrong on the loop thread**, where it would stop the loop. On the loop thread use `try_write`,
which never waits and fails with `WouldBlock` when the buffer is full:

```rust
use simoom::{Outcome, Reply, Request};

fn small(_: &mut Request<'_>, reply: Reply<'_>) -> Outcome {
    let mut sink = reply.stream();
    // on the loop thread: try_write never waits
    let _ = sink.try_write(b"first part, ");
    let _ = sink.try_write(b"second part");
    sink.finish();
    Outcome::Done
}
```

`BodySink` also has `poll_ready` and a `ready()` future for code that runs its own executor; no
runtime is attached.

Ending the body:

- `finish()`, or dropping the sink, ends it normally.
- `finish_with_trailers(&[("grpc-status", "0")])` ends it with trailer fields (trailing HEADERS on
  HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, a trailer section on HTTP/1.1).
- `abort()` cuts it off: the HTTP/1.1 connection closes, or the HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 stream is reset,
  so the client knows the body is incomplete.
- `is_closed()` tells you the client is gone; `write` then fails with `BrokenPipe`.

```rust
use simoom::{Outcome, Reply, Request};

fn grpc_like(_: &mut Request<'_>, reply: Reply<'_>) -> Outcome {
    let mut sink = reply.header("content-type", "application/grpc").stream();
    std::thread::spawn(move || {
        let _ = sink.write(b"\0\0\0\0\0");
        sink.finish_with_trailers(&[("grpc-status", "0")]);
    });
    Outcome::Done
}
```

## Server-sent events

`reply.sse()` is `stream()` with `content-type: text/event-stream` and `cache-control: no-cache`.
`send_event` writes one event: each line of the text becomes a `data:` line, followed by a blank
line.

```rust
use simoom::{Outcome, Reply, Request, Router};
use std::time::Duration;

fn router() -> Router {
    Router::new().get("/events", |_: &mut Request<'_>, r: Reply<'_>| -> Outcome {
        let mut sink = r.sse();
        std::thread::spawn(move || {
            for i in 0.. {
                if sink.send_event(&format!("tick {i}")).is_err() {
                    return; // the browser closed the page
                }
                std::thread::sleep(Duration::from_secs(1));
            }
        });
        Outcome::Done
    })
}
```

In the browser, `new EventSource("/events")` receives the ticks. For named events or ids, write
the fields yourself with `sink.write(b"event: update\ndata: ...\n\n")`.

A thread per stream is simple and fine for tens or hundreds of streams. For many thousands, keep
the sinks in one place and have a single thread (or a timer) write to all of them.

Long-lived streams over HTTP/2 can outlive a client that vanished without closing its
connection. The `h2-keepalive` feature with `Limits::h2_keepalive` sends PINGs to find such
clients ([HTTP/2 and HTTP/3](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/http2-and-http3.html)).

## Request bodies

Bodies up to `Limits::body_buffer` (64 KiB by default) are read whole before your service is
called, and `req.body()` returns them:

```rust
use simoom::{Outcome, Reply, Request};

fn upload(req: &mut Request<'_>, reply: Reply<'_>) -> Outcome {
    if req.is_streamed() {
        return reply.status(413).body_static(b"send less than 64 KiB here");
    }
    let n = req.body().len();
    reply.body(format!("got {n} bytes"))
}
```

Larger bodies, and bodies of unknown length, stream: `req.is_streamed()` is true, `req.body()` is
empty, and `req.take_body()` returns a `BodySource`. The connection reads from the socket only
while the source has room, so a slow reader slows the client down (pull-based backpressure).

`BodySource` implements `std::io::Read`, which blocks, so read it on the offload pool or your own
thread:

```rust
use simoom::{blocking, OwnedRequest, Response};
use std::io::Read;

fn service() -> impl simoom::Service {
    blocking(|mut req: OwnedRequest| {
        let mut total = 0u64;
        if let Some(mut body) = req.take_body() {
            let mut buf = [0u8; 16 * 1024];
            loop {
                match body.read(&mut buf) {
                    Ok(0) => break,
                    Ok(n) => total += n as u64, // hash it, write it to disk, ...
                    Err(_) => return Response::new(400).body("upload broken off"),
                }
            }
        } else {
            total = req.body().len() as u64;
        }
        Response::text(format!("received {total} bytes"))
    })
}
```

When you just want the whole body, `OwnedRequest::read_body()` returns the buffered body or reads
the stream to its end:

```rust
use simoom::{blocking, OwnedRequest, Response};

fn service() -> impl simoom::Service {
    blocking(|mut req: OwnedRequest| match req.read_body() {
        Ok(body) => Response::text(format!("{} bytes", body.len())),
        Err(_) => Response::new(400).body("bad body"),
    })
}
```

`BodySource::try_read` and `poll_read` don't block, if you need to read on the loop thread.
Trailers of a streamed body are available from `BodySource::trailers()` once it is complete.

Limits that apply to request bodies:

- `Limits::max_body` (10 MiB): a larger `Content-Length` is refused with `413` before any body
  byte is read; a chunked body that grows past it fails the read.
- `Limits::min_body_rate` (1 KiB/s after a 5-second grace): a client that sends slower is cut off.

## Common questions

### Can I stream a file to the client?

Yes: open it on your own thread or an offload worker and copy it into the sink with
`std::io::copy(&mut file, &mut sink)`. simoom has no static-file server, so paths, content types
and range requests are up to you (the `conditional` feature helps with ETags and ranges).

### Does SSE work over HTTP/2 and HTTP/3?

Yes. The same `sse()` call works on every protocol; on HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 many event streams share
one connection.

### How do I know the client disconnected?

`write` and `send_event` return an error, and `is_closed()` returns true. Stop producing and drop
the sink.

### Can response compression apply to streams?

Yes, with the `compression` feature and `Compression::new().streams(true)`; each compressed
stream then holds a compressor of about 256 KiB while it runs.

---

Source: https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/websocket.html

# How do I accept WebSocket connections with simoom?

> Implement `WebSocketHandler` and answer with `reply.websocket(handler)`; the handler runs on the loop thread, and a `WsHandle` sends from other threads.

WebSocket is on by default (feature `websocket`) for HTTP/1.1. The same handler also serves
WebSocket over HTTP/2 with the `websocket-h2` feature and over HTTP/3 with `websocket-h3`.

## An echo server

```rust
use simoom::{Reply, Request, Router, Server, WebSocket, WebSocketHandler, WsMessage};

struct Echo;

impl WebSocketHandler for Echo {
    fn on_message(&mut self, ws: &mut WebSocket<'_>, msg: WsMessage<'_>) {
        match msg {
            WsMessage::Text(text) => ws.send_text(text),
            WsMessage::Binary(bytes) => ws.send_binary(bytes),
        }
    }
}

fn main() {
    let router = Router::new().get("/ws", |_: &mut Request<'_>, r: Reply<'_>| r.websocket(Echo));
    let server = Server::builder().listen("127.0.0.1:8080").service(router).start().unwrap();
    server.join();
}
```

`reply.websocket(handler)` sends the `101 Switching Protocols` and hands the connection to the
handler. A request that isn't a valid WebSocket handshake gets `400`.

## The handler

`WebSocketHandler` has three callbacks:

| callback | when |
|---|---|
| `on_open(&mut self, ws)` | the upgrade completed (optional) |
| `on_message(&mut self, ws, msg)` | a whole message arrived; fragments are joined for you |
| `on_close(&mut self, code, reason)` | the connection is closing: the peer's code, 1005 if it sent none, 1006 if the connection was lost (optional) |

Inside a callback, `ws` sends with `send_text`, `send_binary` and `ping`, closes with
`close(code, reason)`, and gives you a `WsHandle` with `handle()`. Pings from the client are
answered automatically.

The handler runs on the loop thread, like a service, so the same rule applies: **no blocking in
callbacks**. Hand slow work to a thread and answer through a `WsHandle`. A panic in a callback
closes that WebSocket with code 1011.

Messages are limited to `Limits::max_ws_message` (1 MiB by default); a larger one closes the
connection with 1009.

## Sending from other threads: a chat room

A `WsHandle` is cheap to clone and can be sent to any thread. `send_text` returns `false` once
the connection is closed, which makes cleanup easy:

```rust
use simoom::{Reply, Request, Router, WebSocket, WebSocketHandler, WsHandle, WsMessage};
use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};

type Room = Arc<Mutex<Vec<WsHandle>>>;

struct Member {
    room: Room,
}

impl WebSocketHandler for Member {
    fn on_open(&mut self, ws: &mut WebSocket<'_>) {
        ws.send_text("welcome");
        self.room.lock().unwrap().push(ws.handle());
    }

    fn on_message(&mut self, _ws: &mut WebSocket<'_>, msg: WsMessage<'_>) {
        if let WsMessage::Text(text) = msg {
            // send_text returns false for a closed connection: drop those handles
            self.room.lock().unwrap().retain(|h| h.send_text(text));
        }
    }

    fn on_close(&mut self, code: u16, _reason: &str) {
        println!("a member left with code {code}");
    }
}

fn router() -> Router {
    let room: Room = Arc::default();
    Router::new().get("/chat", move |_: &mut Request<'_>, r: Reply<'_>| r.websocket(Member { room: room.clone() }))
}
```

A background thread can push to a client the same way:

```rust
use simoom::WsHandle;
use std::time::Duration;

fn push_clock(handle: WsHandle) {
    std::thread::spawn(move || {
        let mut n = 0u64;
        while handle.send_text(format!("tick {n}")) {
            n += 1;
            std::thread::sleep(Duration::from_secs(1));
        }
    });
}
```

`WsHandle` has `send_text`, `send_binary`, `ping` and `close`.

## Subprotocols

When the client offers subprotocols in `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`, pick one with
`websocket_with_protocol`:

```rust
use simoom::{Outcome, Reply, Request, WebSocket, WebSocketHandler, WsMessage};

struct Graphql;
impl WebSocketHandler for Graphql {
    fn on_message(&mut self, _ws: &mut WebSocket<'_>, _msg: WsMessage<'_>) {}
}

fn handler(req: &mut Request<'_>, reply: Reply<'_>) -> Outcome {
    if !req.is_websocket_upgrade() {
        return reply.status(426).header("upgrade", "websocket").empty();
    }
    let offered = req.header("sec-websocket-protocol").unwrap_or(b"");
    let wants = offered.split(|&b| b == b',').any(|p| p.trim_ascii() == b"graphql-transport-ws");
    let protocol = if wants { Some("graphql-transport-ws") } else { None };
    reply.websocket_with_protocol(protocol, Graphql)
}
```

Check `Origin`, cookies or a token in the request before you accept: the upgrade request is an
ordinary request until you call `websocket`.

## Compression and other protocols

| feature | adds |
|---|---|
| `websocket` (default), alias `ws` | WebSocket over HTTP/1.1 (RFC 6455) |
| `ws-deflate` | permessage-deflate compression (RFC 7692), offered with `Builder::websocket_deflate` |
| `websocket-h2` | WebSocket over HTTP/2 (RFC 8441), many sockets on one connection |
| `websocket-h3` | WebSocket over HTTP/3 (RFC 9220) |

None of the last three is in `default` or `full`, to keep those builds within their size
budgets. With `ws-deflate`:

```rust
use simoom::{Server, WsDeflate};

fn build() -> simoom::Builder {
    Server::builder().listen("127.0.0.1:8080").websocket_deflate(WsDeflate::default())
}
```

Each compressing WebSocket holds about 330 KiB of codec state, so offer deflate only when the
messages compress well and the number of connections is moderate.

## Common questions

### Can I use simoom for a WebSocket server in a CLI or desktop app?

Yes. That's a good fit: a command-line tool or desktop app can start a server on `127.0.0.1:0`,
open the browser on the printed port, and push updates over WebSocket or SSE, without pulling an
async runtime into a program that never needed one.

### Is there a WebSocket client?

Yes, in the separate `simoom-client` crate: `client.websocket("ws://...").connect()`. See
[The client](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/client.html).

### How many WebSocket connections can one server hold?

Idle connections cost little: in benchmark campaign 4 (2026-11-12), an idle HTTP connection took
573 bytes with 10,000 open and 532 bytes with 100,000 open (see the
[benchmarks](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/benchmarks/)). Real limits come
from your handler's state, compression, and `Limits::max_connections`.

### Do I need to answer pings?

No. Pings are answered automatically, and `ws.ping(...)` sends your own.

---

Source: https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/tls.html

# How do I serve HTTPS with simoom?

> Turn on the `tls` feature, load your certificate into a `ServerConfig`, and call `listen_tls` and `tls`; simoom does TLS 1.3 itself, with no OpenSSL.

simoom has its own TLS 1.3 implementation, with its own cryptography, in the `simoom-tls` crate.
There is nothing to install and nothing to link. This page covers certificates, several names on
one server, rotation without restart, and client certificates.

## Turn it on

```toml
simoom = { version = "0.1", features = ["tls"] }   # or "full" for TLS and HTTP/3
```

`tls` supports X25519 and P-256 key exchange, ECDSA P-256 and RSA certificates, and AES-GCM.
`tls-extra` adds P-384 and Ed25519 certificates and ChaCha20-Poly1305.

## A self-signed certificate for local testing

`simoom::tls::certgen` makes certificates for tests:

```rust
use simoom::tls::{certgen, ServerConfig, CertifiedKey};
use simoom::{Reply, Request, Server};

fn main() {
    let cert = certgen::self_signed("localhost");
    let key = CertifiedKey::from_pem(cert.cert_pem.as_bytes(), cert.key_pem.as_bytes()).expect("certificate and key");
    let server = Server::builder()
        .listen_tls("127.0.0.1:8443")
        .tls(ServerConfig::new(key))
        .service(|_: &mut Request<'_>, r: Reply<'_>| r.body_static(b"Hello over TLS"))
        .start()
        .unwrap();
    server.join();
}
```

`curl -k https://localhost:8443/` connects (`-k` because the certificate is self-signed). The
`localhost` certificate also covers `127.0.0.1` and `::1`.

## Your own certificate

Load a PEM chain and key, for example from Let's Encrypt. Keys in PKCS#8, SEC1 or PKCS#1 form
work. Plain and TLS listeners can live on one server:

```rust
use simoom::tls::ServerConfig;
use simoom::{Reply, Request, Server};

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let cert = std::fs::read("/etc/simoom/fullchain.pem")?;
    let key = std::fs::read("/etc/simoom/privkey.pem")?;
    let tls = ServerConfig::from_pem(&cert, &key).map_err(|e| format!("{e:?}"))?;

    let server = Server::builder()
        .listen("0.0.0.0:80") // plain HTTP on one port
        .listen_tls("0.0.0.0:443") // TLS on another
        .tls(tls)
        .service(|req: &mut Request<'_>, r: Reply<'_>| r.body(format!("secure: {}", req.is_secure())))
        .start()?;
    server.join();
    Ok(())
}
```

On a TLS listener, client and server agree on HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1 during the handshake (ALPN).
`Builder::tls` sets the ALPN list for you. For HTTP/3, see [HTTP/2 and HTTP/3](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/http2-and-http3.html).

## Several names on one server

`add_sni_cert` adds a certificate that is chosen when the client asks for one of its names (SNI),
wildcards included. Clients asking for other names get the default certificate:

```rust
use simoom::tls::{CertifiedKey, ServerConfig};

fn config(a: CertifiedKey, b: CertifiedKey) -> ServerConfig {
    let mut tls = ServerConfig::new(a); // the default certificate
    tls.add_sni_cert(b); // chosen when the client asks for one of its names
    tls
}
```

Set `tls.strict_sni = true` to refuse clients whose name matches no certificate.

## Rotating certificates without a restart

`ServerHandle::set_tls` swaps the configuration. New connections use it; open ones keep theirs:

```rust
use simoom::tls::ServerConfig;
use simoom::ServerHandle;

fn reload(server: &ServerHandle) -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let cert = std::fs::read("/etc/simoom/fullchain.pem")?;
    let key = std::fs::read("/etc/simoom/privkey.pem")?;
    let tls = ServerConfig::from_pem(&cert, &key).map_err(|e| format!("{e:?}"))?;
    server.set_tls(tls)?; // new connections use it; open ones keep theirs
    Ok(())
}
```

`set_quic_tls` does the same for HTTP/3. Session tickets issued before the swap resume only if
the new configuration shares the old one's `ticketer`.

## Client certificates (mutual TLS)

Require or request client certificates with `ServerConfig::client_auth`. The `ClientAuth` and
`RootStore` types live in `simoom-tls`, which `simoom` doesn't re-export in 0.1.0, so add it
next to simoom (`cargo add simoom-tls`, same version):

```rust
use simoom::tls::ServerConfig;
use simoom::{Outcome, Reply, Request};
use simoom_tls::x509::RootStore;
use simoom_tls::ClientAuth;

fn config(mut tls: ServerConfig) -> Result<ServerConfig, String> {
    let mut roots = RootStore::empty();
    roots.add_pem_file("/etc/simoom/client-ca.pem")?;
    tls.client_auth = ClientAuth::Required(roots);
    Ok(tls)
}

fn whoami(req: &mut Request<'_>, reply: Reply<'_>) -> Outcome {
    match req.tls() {
        Some(info) if !info.peer_certificates().is_empty() => {
            reply.body(format!("client certificate of {} bytes, {}", info.peer_certificates()[0].len(), info.cipher_suite_name()))
        }
        _ => reply.status(401).empty(),
    }
}
```

`ClientAuth::Optional(roots)` asks for a certificate but accepts clients without one; the ones
that send one are still verified. `req.tls()` also gives the protocol version, cipher suite, the
SNI name and the negotiated ALPN protocol.

## What simoom's TLS does and doesn't do

- **TLS 1.3 only** on simoom servers. TLS 1.2 exists in `simoom-tls` behind its `tls12` feature,
  but simoom's features don't turn it on. Clients that only speak TLS 1.2 fail the handshake.
- **0-RTT is never accepted**, by design: early data can be replayed.
- **Session resumption** with tickets is on by default, with rotating keys.
- **Constant-time crypto**: hardware AES-GCM where the CPU has it, a bitsliced fallback elsewhere,
  constant-time comparison of secrets.
- **The handshake deadline** is `Limits::head_timeout` (10 s by default).
- **Not independently audited yet.** The TLS stack passed testssl.sh and interop with OpenSSL,
  curl, Python, GnuTLS and Schannel ([SECURITY.md](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/SECURITY.html)), but no outside firm has
  audited it. If your rules require an audited stack, terminate TLS in front of simoom.

## Common questions

### Do I need OpenSSL, a C compiler or cmake?

No. simoom's TLS and cryptography are Rust code in the repository, so cross-compiling for another
target needs only the Rust target.

### Can I use rustls or OpenSSL instead?

Not inside simoom's listeners. You can put a TLS terminator (nginx, haproxy, a cloud load
balancer) in front of a plain simoom listener; HTTP/2 with prior knowledge (h2c) is a good
protocol between them.

### How do I redirect HTTP to HTTPS?

Listen on both ports and answer plain requests with a redirect:
`if !req.is_secure() { return r.status(308).header("location", url).empty(); }`.

### Does TLS make start-up slower?

A little. In benchmark campaign 4 (2026-11-12), the full server, with TLS 1.3 and HTTP/3, gave its
first answer 1.49 ms after start, against 0.94 ms for the default build without them; hyper,
without TLS, took 1.48 ms on the same droplet. Part of the difference is HTTP/3, which starts every
event loop at once ([benchmarks](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/benchmarks/)).

---

Source: https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/http2-and-http3.html

# How do I serve HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 with simoom?

> HTTP/2 is on by default (h2c on plain listeners, ALPN over TLS); for HTTP/3 build with `full` and add `listen_quic` with `quic_tls` on the same port number.

Your services don't change between protocols: the same `Request` and `Reply` work on HTTP/1.1,
HTTP/2 and HTTP/3. What changes is which listeners you open and a few limits.

## One server, every protocol

```rust
use simoom::tls::{certgen, CertifiedKey, ServerConfig};
use simoom::{Reply, Request, Server, Version};

fn main() {
    let cert = certgen::self_signed("localhost");
    let key = CertifiedKey::from_pem(cert.cert_pem.as_bytes(), cert.key_pem.as_bytes()).unwrap();
    let tls = ServerConfig::new(key);

    let server = Server::builder()
        .listen("0.0.0.0:8080") // HTTP/1.1 and h2c
        .listen_tls("0.0.0.0:8443") // HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, chosen by ALPN
        .tls(tls.clone())
        .listen_quic("0.0.0.0:8443") // HTTP/3 on the same port number, over UDP
        .quic_tls(tls)
        .service(|req: &mut Request<'_>, r: Reply<'_>| {
            let v = match req.version() {
                Version::H3 => "HTTP/3",
                Version::H2 => "HTTP/2",
                _ => "HTTP/1.x",
            };
            r.body(format!("you came over {v}\n"))
        })
        .start()
        .unwrap();
    println!("TCP {:?}, UDP {:?}", server.local_addrs(), server.quic_addrs());
    server.join();
}
```

Build it with `--features full` (or `tls` and `http3`). Then:

```sh
curl --http2-prior-knowledge http://localhost:8080/   # h2c
curl -k --http2 https://localhost:8443/                # h2 over TLS
curl -k --http3-only https://localhost:8443/           # HTTP/3, with a curl built for it
```

## HTTP/2

With the default `http2` feature, simoom speaks HTTP/2 three ways:

- **h2c with prior knowledge** on plain listeners: the client starts with the HTTP/2 preface.
  This is the recommended protocol between a proxy and simoom, since it has none of HTTP/1.1's
  framing ambiguities.
- **`Upgrade: h2c`** from an HTTP/1.1 request on plain listeners.
- **h2 over TLS**, chosen in the handshake (ALPN).

`Builder::http2(false)` turns it off for one server. h2spec 2.6.0 passes 146 of 146 tests
([SECURITY.md](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/SECURITY.html)).

## HTTP/3

HTTP/3 runs over QUIC on UDP. `listen_quic(addr)` opens a UDP listener, and `quic_tls(config)`
gives it a TLS configuration (its ALPN becomes `h3`). It is usual to use the same port number as
the TLS listener, since TCP and UDP ports are separate.

Browsers find HTTP/3 through the **`alt-svc`** header: once a QUIC listener is open, HTTP/1.1 and
HTTP/2 responses carry `alt-svc: h3=":<port>"; ma=86400`, and the browser switches on a later
request. If a load balancer forwards UDP on another public port, set the value yourself with
`Builder::alt_svc`.

What simoom's QUIC does not do in 0.1.0:

- **No 0-RTT**, by design (early data can be replayed).
- **No ECN** and **no migration to a preferred address**.
- It is a transport for HTTP/3, not a general QUIC library: there are no raw QUIC streams in the
  `simoom` API.

In the QUIC Interop Runner, simoom passes 54 of 58 supported pairs against the ngtcp2, quiche and
quic-go clients; the four failures are 0-RTT and ECN.

## Tuning

```rust
use simoom::{FrameBudgets, Limits, Server};
use std::time::Duration;

fn build() -> simoom::Builder {
    Server::builder()
        .listen("127.0.0.1:8080")
        .http2(false) // HTTP/1.1 only on this server
        .alt_svc(r#"h3=":443"; ma=3600"#) // when a load balancer owns the UDP port
        .limits(Limits {
            max_concurrent_streams: 250,
            h2_frame_budgets: FrameBudgets { ping: 50, ..FrameBudgets::default() },
            h2_keepalive: Some(Duration::from_secs(30)), // feature h2-keepalive
            ..Limits::default()
        })
        .quic_config(|c| c.retry = true) // always validate client addresses with Retry
}
```

| setting | default | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `Limits::max_concurrent_streams` | 100 | streams per connection whose handler is still running; more get `REFUSED_STREAM` |
| `Limits::max_header_list` | 16 KiB | the decoded header block of one request |
| `Limits::header_table_size` | 4096 | the HPACK and QPACK dynamic table |
| `Limits::h2_frame_budgets` | see [Limits and security](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/limits-and-security.html) | caps RST_STREAM, PING, SETTINGS and other frame floods |
| `Limits::h2_keepalive` | off | PINGs idle clients to find ones that vanished (feature `h2-keepalive`) |
| `Builder::quic_config` | | QUIC transport settings: Retry, connection caps, versions |
| `Builder::quic_gro(false)` | on | turns off UDP receive batching on Linux |

`max_concurrent_streams` counts streams whose handler is still working, not just open streams, so
resetting streams can't free capacity while work continues. That is the defence against Rapid
Reset (CVE-2023-44487) and MadeYouReset (CVE-2025-8671).

## Common questions

### Can I serve HTTP/3 from Rust without quinn, rustls or OpenSSL?

Yes. simoom implements QUIC v1, HTTP/3, QPACK and TLS 1.3 itself, and HTTP/3 is a cargo feature
of the same server that serves HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2.

### Do I need a certificate for HTTP/3?

Yes. QUIC always uses TLS 1.3, so `listen_quic` needs `quic_tls`; starting without one is an
error.

### Why do browsers keep using HTTP/2 the first time?

Browsers learn about HTTP/3 from the `alt-svc` header of an earlier response, then switch. Also
check that UDP on that port is open in your firewall.

### Does HTTP/3 change my handlers?

No. `req.version()` tells you the protocol if you want to know; everything else is the same,
including streaming and server-sent events. WebSocket over HTTP/3 needs the `websocket-h3`
feature.

---

Source: https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/limits-and-security.html

# What does simoom limit and refuse, and how do I change it?

> Every resource has a limit in `simoom::Limits` with a safe default; ambiguous requests are refused, and a panicking handler becomes a 500, not a crash.

simoom is built to face the internet directly. This page lists the limits you are most likely to
change, what the server refuses on its own, and how to see what happened. The full security
model, every default and the test results are in [SECURITY.md](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/SECURITY.html).

## Changing limits

`Limits` is a plain struct. Change the fields you care about and keep the defaults for the rest:

```rust
use simoom::{Limits, Server};
use std::time::Duration;

fn build() -> simoom::Builder {
    Server::builder().listen("0.0.0.0:8080").limits(Limits {
        max_body: 1 << 20,                       // 1 MiB uploads, 413 beyond
        max_headers: 50,                         // 431 beyond
        head_timeout: Duration::from_secs(5),    // slowloris
        keep_alive_timeout: Duration::from_secs(30),
        max_connections_per_ip: 256,             // only when clients are not behind one NAT
        reconnect_rate: 50,                      // new connections per second per IP
        ..Limits::default()
    })
}
```

## The limits you'll most often touch

| field | default | when exceeded |
|---|---|---|
| `max_request_line` | 8 KiB | `414` |
| `max_head` / `max_headers` / `max_header_line` | 16 KiB / 100 / 8 KiB | `431` |
| `max_body` | 10 MiB, checked against `Content-Length` before any body byte is read | `413` |
| `body_buffer` | 64 KiB; larger bodies stream | — |
| `head_timeout` | 10 s for the whole request head (also the TLS handshake) | close |
| `keep_alive_timeout` | 15 s idle between requests | close |
| `min_body_rate` / `body_rate_grace` | 1 KiB/s after 5 s | close |
| `write_timeout` | 30 s without the client reading | close |
| `defer_timeout` | off | `504` for a deferred or offloaded reply |
| `max_connections` / `max_connections_per_loop` | about a million each | accepted and closed at once |
| `max_connections_per_ip` / `reconnect_rate` | off | accepted and closed at once |
| `max_concurrent_streams` | 100 per HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 connection | `REFUSED_STREAM` |
| `max_ws_message` | 1 MiB | WebSocket close 1009 |
| `offload_threads` / `offload_queue` | 32 per CPU (512 to 1024) / 4096 | `503` with `Retry-After` |

The per-IP limits are off by default because, behind a proxy or a NAT, every client shares one
address. Turn them on only when clients connect to simoom directly.

## What simoom refuses on its own

Parsing follows RFC 9110, 9112, 9113, 9114 and 9204 strictly. Requests whose framing could be
read two ways are refused, and the connection closes, so a proxy in front can't be tricked into
seeing different request boundaries (request smuggling). Among others:

- both `Transfer-Encoding` and `Content-Length`, duplicate or malformed `Content-Length`, any
  transfer coding other than a single final `chunked`;
- bare CR or LF line endings, folded headers, control bytes, whitespace before a colon;
- a request target with user information (`http://user@host/`).

`CONNECT` is answered by your service and then the connection closes: simoom is never a tunnel.
In tests behind nginx and haproxy, and in the HTTP Garden next to nginx, Apache httpd, h2o,
hyper, gunicorn and Go, simoom showed no desyncs ([SECURITY.md](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/SECURITY.html)).

## Attacks it defends against

- **Slowloris** (heads sent byte by byte): `head_timeout`. A slow head holds no buffer, so while
  the server has connections to spare it stays open up to `slow_head_limit` (300 s), because
  closing it early only makes the attacker reconnect.
- **Slow POST and slow read**: `min_body_rate` and `write_timeout`.
- **HTTP/2 floods** (Rapid Reset, MadeYouReset, PING, SETTINGS and empty-frame floods): frame
  budgets per connection; going over one closes the connection with `ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM`.
- **Reconnect storms**: `reconnect_rate` per IP.
- **Overload**: the offload pool answers `503` early instead of queueing. Opt-in admission control
  (`shed_lag`, `max_pending_per_loop` with `pending_503`) can shed new requests when a loop falls
  behind.
- **QUIC**: Retry under handshake load, the 3x amplification limit, bounded buffers.

The `guard` feature (on by default) carries the overload and slow-client guards; an edge build
that leaves it out also ignores those limits.

## Panics

A panic in a service becomes a `500`, the connection closes, and the server keeps running. A
panic in a WebSocket callback closes that WebSocket with 1011. Both are counted in
`stats().panics`.

## Seeing what happened

`Builder::on_complete` is called once for every finished request, including requests the parser
refused, with the status, byte counts, duration, protocol and peer. It runs on the loop thread, so
keep it quick; send the record to a channel for real logging:

```rust
use simoom::{Completion, Server};

fn build() -> simoom::Builder {
    Server::builder()
        .listen("0.0.0.0:8080")
        .on_complete(|c: &Completion| {
            // runs on the loop thread: keep it quick (push to a channel for real logging)
            if c.status >= 500 {
                eprintln!("{:?} {} {} µs peer={:?}", c.version, c.status, c.duration.as_micros(), c.peer);
            }
        })
        .log(|line| eprintln!("simoom: {line}"))
}
```

`Builder::log` decides where simoom's own log lines (stall warnings) go; the default is standard
error. Counters for every limit are in `ServerHandle::stats()`:

```rust
use simoom::ServerHandle;

fn report(server: &ServerHandle) {
    let s = server.stats();
    println!(
        "open {} requests {} bad {} too large {} timeouts {} panics {} stalls {} 503s {}",
        s.active, s.requests, s.bad_requests, s.too_large, s.timeouts, s.panics, s.stalls, s.overloaded
    );
}
```

## Honest limits

- simoom 0.1.0 has **not had an independent security audit**. The testing listed in
  [SECURITY.md](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/SECURITY.html) (h2spec, the QUIC Interop Runner, HTTP Garden, testssl.sh,
  fuzzing) was done by the project.
- simoom is an origin server. It is not a reverse proxy, a forward proxy or a static-file server,
  so the protections of those roles are not its job.

## Common questions

### Is simoom safe to put on the internet?

It was built for that: strict parsing, a limit on everything, flood and slow-client defences,
and panics contained. It has no outside audit yet, so weigh that for high-risk deployments; see
[SECURITY.md](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/SECURITY.html).

### Does simoom use unsafe code?

Only in one crate, `simoom-sys`, which holds the operating-system calls, SIMD and crypto
intrinsics; each `unsafe` block there documents why it is sound. Every other crate is
`#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`. There are no third-party crates at all.

### How do I report a vulnerability?

Privately, through [GitHub security advisories](https://github.com/Cameleering/simoom/security/advisories/new),
as described in [SECURITY.md](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/SECURITY.html).

### Can I turn off certificate verification in the client?

No. To trust a self-signed server, add its certificate to the client's root store
([The client](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/client.html)).

---

Source: https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/runtime.html

# How do I set simoom's threads, I/O back end and shutdown?

> simoom runs one event loop per CPU core by default; set `threads`, pick a `Backend`, and stop with `stop(grace)` followed by `join()`.

simoom has its own runtime, not tokio. Each loop thread owns its connections from accept to close
and shares nothing with the others, so there are no locks on the request path. This page covers
the settings you can change.

## Threads and back ends

```rust
use simoom::{Backend, Reply, Request, Server};
use std::time::Duration;

fn main() {
    let server = Server::builder()
        .listen("0.0.0.0:8080")
        .threads(2) // 0 (the default) = one loop per CPU
        .backend(Backend::IoUring) // Linux 6.1+; falls back to epoll
        .service(|_: &mut Request<'_>, r: Reply<'_>| r.body_static(b"ok"))
        .start()
        .unwrap();
    println!("back end {:?}, fallback: {:?}", server.backend(), server.fallback_reason());
    // ...
    server.stop(Duration::from_secs(5));
    server.join();
}
```

**Threads.** `threads(0)`, the default, starts one loop per CPU the process may use. Only the
first loop starts at once; the others start in the background once traffic arrives, so an idle
server or a serverless instance pays for one thread (with an HTTP/3 listener every loop starts at
once). On machines with 4 or more CPUs where the network card's receive work lands on one CPU,
the default uses one loop fewer and keeps the loops off that CPU.

**Back ends.**

| `Backend` | platform |
|---|---|
| `Auto` (default) | epoll on Linux, IOCP on Windows, kqueue on macOS and BSD |
| `Epoll` | Linux, edge-triggered |
| `IoUring` | Linux 6.1 and newer, with the `io-uring` feature (on by default); falls back to epoll when the kernel refuses it |
| `Iocp` | Windows completion ports |
| `Kqueue` | macOS and BSD |

The environment variable `SIMOOM_BACKEND` (`epoll`, `io_uring`, `iocp`, `kqueue`) chooses the back
end when the code says `Auto`, which is handy for trying io_uring without a rebuild.
`server.fallback_reason()` tells you why io_uring was replaced, if it was.

Which is faster depends on the load: in the committed benchmarks epoll led at 64 and 256
connections and io_uring at 1,024 ([benchmarks](https://cameleer.ing/simoom/benchmarks/)).

## Graceful stop

`server.stop(grace)` closes the listeners, then:

- idle HTTP/1.1 connections close at once, busy ones after their response, with
  `Connection: close`;
- HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 connections get `GOAWAY` and close when their streams finish;
- whatever is still open after `grace` is aborted.

`server.join()` waits for the loops to exit. Dropping the `ServerHandle` stops at once, without a
grace period.

simoom doesn't install signal handlers. Wire your own shutdown signal to `stop`:

```rust
use simoom::{Reply, Request, Server};
use std::time::Duration;

fn run() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let server = Server::builder()
        .listen("0.0.0.0:8080")
        .service(|_: &mut Request<'_>, r: Reply<'_>| r.body_static(b"ok"))
        .start()?;
    // block until stdin closes, a stand-in for your own shutdown signal
    let _ = std::io::Read::read_to_end(&mut std::io::stdin(), &mut Vec::new());
    server.stop(Duration::from_secs(10));
    server.join();
    Ok(())
}
```

## Existing listeners

`Server::from_listeners` serves sockets you already have: socket activation by systemd, a port
handed over from a parent process, or a listener bound before dropping privileges.
`listen_on` and `listen_on_tls` add one at a time:

```rust
use simoom::{Reply, Request, Server};
use std::net::TcpListener;

fn run() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let listener = TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:0")?;
    let server = Server::from_listeners(vec![listener])
        .service(|_: &mut Request<'_>, r: Reply<'_>| r.body_static(b"ok"))
        .start()?;
    server.join();
    Ok(())
}
```

## Low-level runtime settings

`Builder::runtime` gives access to the runtime configuration: CPU pinning, buffer sizes, thread
names, stack size, lingering close and more. Most programs never need it:

```rust
use simoom::Server;

fn build() -> simoom::Builder {
    Server::builder().listen("0.0.0.0:8080").runtime(|rt| {
        rt.pin_threads = true; // loop i on CPU i
        rt.thread_name = "web".into();
    })
}
```

The fields are documented on `simoom_rt::Config` at [docs.rs/simoom-rt](https://docs.rs/simoom-rt).

## Counters

`server.stats()` returns a `Stats` snapshot: connections accepted, rejected and open, requests,
refusals by kind, timeouts, panics, watchdog stalls, `503`s, upgrades, TLS errors, the offload
pool's counters and per-loop runtime counters. Each loop writes only its own counters, so they
cost nothing on the request path. Expose them however you like, for example on a `/metrics`
route.

## Common questions

### Should I use io_uring?

Try both on your workload. `Auto` uses epoll on Linux; in the committed runs epoll led at 64 and
256 connections and io_uring at 1,024. Setting `SIMOOM_BACKEND=io_uring`
lets you compare without a rebuild.

### How many threads should I use?

The default, one per CPU, suits a server. On a shared machine, or inside an app that does other
work, set fewer. A serverless function serving one request at a time effectively uses one loop,
since the others start only under load.

### Does simoom run on macOS and ARM?

macOS (kqueue) and the ARM code paths compile and are checked in the build, but the test suite
runs on Windows and Linux and the benchmarks ran on x86-64. Reports from macOS and ARM are welcome.

### Can I run two servers in one process?

Yes. Each `Server::builder().start()` creates its own loops, listeners and connections.

---

Source: https://cameleer.ing/simoom/docs/guides/client.html

# How do I make HTTP requests with simoom-client?

> `simoom-client` is a blocking HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 client with pooling, TLS, redirects and WebSocket; add it with `cargo add simoom-client`.

The client is a separate crate, so a server that never makes requests doesn't compile it. Like
the server, it uses only the standard library and needs no async runtime: requests run on the
calling thread, and HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 connections are shared between threads.

```sh
cargo add simoom-client
```

The default features give HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, WebSocket, TLS and gzip/deflate decoding. HTTP/3 needs
`client-h3`; `full` turns on everything (cookies, auth, multipart, retries, proxies over SOCKS...).

## A first request

```rust
use simoom_client::Client;

fn main() -> simoom_client::Result<()> {
    let client = Client::new();
    let resp = client.get("https://example.com/").send()?;
    println!("{} {}", resp.status(), resp.header("content-type").unwrap_or(""));
    let text = resp.text()?;
    println!("{} characters", text.len());
    Ok(())
}
```

Create one `Client` and reuse it: it pools connections per origin. Clone it to use the same pool
from other threads.

## Settings, bodies and versions

```rust
use simoom_client::{Client, HttpVersion};
use std::time::Duration;

fn run() -> simoom_client::Result<()> {
    let client = Client::builder()
        .connect_timeout(Some(Duration::from_secs(5)))
        .timeout(Some(Duration::from_secs(30)))
        .follow_redirects(true)
        .user_agent(Some("my-tool/1.0".into()))
        .build();

    let resp = client
        .post("http://127.0.0.1:8080/orders")
        .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
        .body(r#"{"sku":"A-1","qty":2}"#)
        .version(HttpVersion::Http2) // h2c with prior knowledge
        .timeout(Duration::from_secs(10))
        .send()?;
    println!("{}", resp.status());

    let resp = client.get("https://api.example.com/items").query("page", "2").bearer_auth("token").send()?;
    let bytes = resp.bytes()?;
    Ok(())
}
```

- **Versions.** `HttpVersion::Auto` (the default) uses HTTP/1.1 for `http://` and lets the TLS
  handshake choose HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1 for `https://`. `Http1`, `Http2` and `Http3` force one.
  With `client-h3` and `.alt_svc(true)` on the builder, an origin that announces HTTP/3 is
  reached over HTTP/3 next time.
- **Timeouts.** Connect, TLS handshake, response head, idle read, write, the whole request and
  the wait for a pooled connection each have a setting.
- **Redirects** are off by default; `follow_redirects(true)` turns them on, with credentials
  stripped across origins.
